topics.title: Functions, composites and inverses
points: A function has one \(y\)-value for each \(x\). State the domain (allowed \(x\)) and range (resulting \(y\)).
The composite \(f(g(x))\) exists only if \(\operatorname{ran}(g) \subseteq \operatorname{dom}(f)\).

An inverse \(f^{-1}\) exists only for a one-to-one function: swap \(x\) and \(y\) and solve. Its graph is the reflection of \(f\) in \(y = x\); \(\operatorname{dom}(f^{-1}) = \operatorname{ran}(f)\) and \(\operatorname{ran}(f^{-1}) = \operatorname{dom}(f)\).
Transformations: \(y = a f\big(b(x - h)\big) + k\). Describe them as dilations, reflections, then translations, or as a mapping \((x, y) \to (x', y')\).
Sum or product of functions: the domain is \(\operatorname{dom}(f) \cap \operatorname{dom}(g)\).
topics.explain: Explain why \(y = x^2\) needs a restricted domain to have an inverse function.

topics.title: Solving equations
points: Exponential and log equations: use the log laws; check every solution is in the domain.
Circular equations: find the base angle, then use symmetry (ASTC) and add periods to get all solutions in the domain.
General solution: \(\sin x = a \Rightarrow x = \sin^{-1}(a) + 2n\pi\) or \(x = \pi - \sin^{-1}(a) + 2n\pi\), \(n \in \mathbb{Z}\).
Simultaneous linear equations can have a unique solution, infinitely many, or none.
Use CAS where allowed, but write the set-up.
topics.explain: Explain why \(2\sin x = 1\) has two solutions in \([0, 2\pi]\).

topics.title: Differentiation rules
points: Standard derivatives: \[\begin{aligned} \frac{d}{dx}e^{kx} &= ke^{kx} & \frac{d}{dx}\log_e x &= \frac{1}{x} \\ \frac{d}{dx}\sin(kx) &= k\cos(kx) & \frac{d}{dx}\cos(kx) &= -k\sin(kx) \\ \frac{d}{dx}\tan(kx) &= \frac{k}{\cos^2(kx)} \end{aligned}\]
Chain rule: \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{dy}{du} \times \dfrac{du}{dx}\).
Product rule: \(\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv) = u'v + uv'\). Quotient rule: \(\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right) = \dfrac{u'v - uv'}{v^2}\).
Applications: tangents and normals, stationary points, maximum and minimum problems, rates of change.
Strictly increasing where \(f'(x) > 0\); strictly decreasing where \(f'(x) < 0\).
Linear approximation: \(f(x + h) \approx f(x) + h f'(x)\).
topics.explain: Explain when you would use the chain rule instead of the product rule.

topics.title: Integration and area
points: Standard integrals: \[\begin{aligned} \int e^{kx}\,dx &= \frac{1}{k}e^{kx} + c & \int \frac{1}{x}\,dx &= \log_e|x| + c \\ \int \sin(kx)\,dx &= -\frac{1}{k}\cos(kx) + c & \int \cos(kx)\,dx &= \frac{1}{k}\sin(kx) + c \end{aligned}\]
Definite integral: \(\displaystyle\int_a^b f(x)\,dx = F(b) - F(a)\).
Area between a curve and the \(x\)-axis: split at the \(x\)-intercepts. Regions below the axis give negative integrals, so take their absolute value.
Area between curves: \(\displaystyle\int_a^b \big(f_{\text{upper}}(x) - f_{\text{lower}}(x)\big)\,dx\).
Average value of \(f\) on \([a, b]\): \(\displaystyle\frac{1}{b - a}\int_a^b f(x)\,dx\). The trapezium rule approximates area.
topics.explain: Explain why \(\displaystyle\int_{-1}^{1} x^3\,dx = 0\) even though there is area between the curve and the axis.

qs.q: Find the average value of \(f(x) = x^2\) on \([0, 3]\).

topics.title: Discrete random variables and the binomial distribution
points: A discrete probability distribution has \(0 \le \Pr(X = x) \le 1\) and \(\sum \Pr(X = x) = 1\).
\(\operatorname{E}(X) = \sum x\Pr(X = x)\). \(\operatorname{Var}(X) = \operatorname{E}(X^2) - [\operatorname{E}(X)]^2\). \(\operatorname{sd}(X) = \sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(X)}\).
Binomial \(X \sim \operatorname{Bi}(n, p)\): \(n\) independent trials, each a success with probability \(p\). \[\Pr(X = x) = \binom{n}{x}p^x(1 - p)^{n - x}\]
Binomial mean \(\operatorname{E}(X) = np\); variance \(\operatorname{Var}(X) = np(1 - p)\).
\(\operatorname{E}(aX + b) = a\operatorname{E}(X) + b\); \(\operatorname{Var}(aX + b) = a^2\operatorname{Var}(X)\).
topics.explain: Explain the four conditions that make a situation binomial.

qs.q: \(X\) takes values \(0, 1, 2\) with probabilities \(0.2, 0.5, 0.3\). Find \(\operatorname{E}(X)\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(X)\).

topics.title: Continuous random variables and the normal distribution
points: A probability density function has \(f(x) \ge 0\) and \(\displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x)\,dx = 1\). \(\Pr(a < X < b) = \displaystyle\int_a^b f(x)\,dx\).
\(\operatorname{E}(X) = \displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x f(x)\,dx\). The median \(m\) satisfies \(\displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{m} f(x)\,dx = 0.5\).
Normal distribution \(X \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)\): about 68% within \(\mu \pm \sigma\), 95% within \(\mu \pm 2\sigma\), 99.7% within \(\mu \pm 3\sigma\).
Standardise: \(Z = \dfrac{X - \mu}{\sigma}\), with \(Z \sim N(0, 1)\).
For a continuous variable, \(\Pr(X = a) = 0\).
topics.explain: Explain why \(\Pr(X = 3) = 0\) for a continuous random variable.

qs.q: \(f(x) = kx\) for \(0 \le x \le 2\) (zero elsewhere) is a probability density function. Find \(k\).

topics.title: Sample proportions and confidence intervals
points: The sample proportion \(\hat{p}\) estimates the population proportion \(p\).
For large samples, \(\hat{P}\) is approximately normal with mean \(p\) and standard deviation \(\sqrt{\dfrac{p(1 - p)}{n}}\).
Approximate 95% confidence interval: \[\left(\hat{p} - 1.96\sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}(1 - \hat{p})}{n}},\ \hat{p} + 1.96\sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}(1 - \hat{p})}{n}}\right)\]
Higher confidence gives a wider interval; a larger sample gives a narrower interval.
About 95% of intervals made this way contain \(p\); any single interval either does or does not.
topics.explain: Explain what a 95% confidence interval does and does not tell you.

qs.q: In a sample of \(n = 100\), \(\hat{p} = 0.4\). Find an approximate 95% confidence interval for \(p\).
Quadrupling the sample size makes the margin of error…
qs.e: The margin is proportional to \(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\), and \(\sqrt{4} = 2\).
